title: Newsletter: Our 5-year anniversary, PHP2Shell, Sovereign Tech Resilience relaunch and more
content:
Email newsletter on 29 October: Our 5-year anniversary, PHP2Shell, Sovereign Tech Resilience relaunch and more

On 12 October, we celebrated our five-year anniversary with guests and friends from policy, open source, government, industry, civil society, and academia. It was a wonderful night to look back at our beginnings, and ahead to the future challenges for digital infrastructure and Europe’s digital sovereignty.

The critical vulnerability PHP2Shell sent shockwaves through the internet, reminding us all how important long-term investments into open source components are for our collective security. Good news though: The Sovereign Tech Resilience program has expanded to include four new services: memory safety transition, post-quantum readiness, supply chain security, and Cyber Resilience Act compliance. Applications are open.

If you’d like to find out about these updates as they happen, you can find the Sovereign Tech Agency on Mastodon, LinkedIn, and Bluesky.

title: Preparing the web for post-quantum cryptography
content:
The Sovereign Tech Fund commissions more than €1 million of work to make Let's Encrypt, which secures a large share of the web, ready for quantum computers.

We have committed more than €1 million to prepare the web for post-quantum cryptography, encryption that is designed to withstand quantum computers. Through the Sovereign Tech Fund, we have contracted the Internet Security Research Group (ISRG) to move Let's Encrypt to Merkle Tree Certificates, a new format for website certificates that stays secure in the quantum era.

Let's Encrypt is the free, automated service that issues website certificates for a large share of the web. A website certificate is a digital document that lets your browser confirm two things: that you reached the website you typed in, and that nobody on the network can read or change what you send.

title: PHP2Shell exposes the funding gap in open-source security
content:
On 21 October 2026, the PHP project released fixes for two critical security vulnerabilities, collectively known as PHP2Shell. Under certain conditions, these vulnerabilities could allow attackers to execute code on affected web servers without authentication.

PHP underpins a substantial share of the web, including public services, businesses, and widely used publishing platforms. The incident highlights a fundamental challenge in open-source security: finding vulnerabilities is only the first step. Fixing them, and preventing similar flaws in the future, requires sustained investment.

In 2024, the Sovereign Tech Agency commissioned the first external security audit of PHP’s core in over a decade, coordinated by OSTIF and conducted by Quarkslab. The audit identified 17 security-related findings and contributed to subsequent work on the underlying problem behind one of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. The organization explicitly recognized the value of this investment.

title: Celebrating five years of strengthening open digital infrastructure
content:
Five years after the feasibility study for investing in the infrastructure of the 21st century, we look back and ahead: how do we strengthen the open source foundation of the future?

Five years ago, the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWi) commissioned a small team to work out, in a feasibility study, how public investment in open digital infrastructure could be designed. In late 2021, the Log4Shell vulnerability in Apache Log4j, a widely used open source software library, caused far-reaching damage. Log4j was running in millions of systems at the time, and the vulnerability spread along software dependencies into public administration systems and critical infrastructure worldwide. The incident exposed a dire situation hiding in plain sight. Open source technologies, from programming libraries and protocols to developer tools and software components, form the technical foundation of all modern digital systems. Yet they suffer from chronic underinvestment, and they are developed and maintained mostly by volunteers. Countless people, companies, and institutions depend on them, but few invest in maintaining them.

title: Sovereign Tech Resilience relaunches with four new services
content:
Sovereign Tech Resilience adds four new services, memory safety transition, post-quantum readiness, supply chain security, and Cyber Resilience Act compliance, and expands two existing services. Applications are open.

The Sovereign Tech Resilience program has been running since 2023, after the German Bundestag allocated funds in the federal budget for a bug bounty program. The program's approach combines hands-on engineering, audits, and bug-and-fix bounties, delivered together with industry partners at no cost to participating free and open source software (FOSS) projects. It helps critical open source projects build better capacity to avoid, absorb, and handle security issues over time.

title: Newsletter: We’re hiring a Director of Technology, supporting memory safety, and kicking off conference season
content:
Email newsletter on 14 September: We’re hiring a Director of Technology, supporting memory safety, and kicking off conference season

There’s a new position open in our leadership team: we’re looking for a Director of Technology to shape and develop the technology strategy of the Sovereign Tech Agency. Together with the German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), we’re endorsing a statement that calls for more support for the large-scale adoption of memory-safe technology, a crucial part of cybersecurity that’s often overlooked. Plus, lots of conferences are coming up where you can meet our team. 

If you’d like to find out about these updates as they happen, you can find the Sovereign Tech Agency on Mastodon, LinkedIn, and Bluesky.

We are looking for a Director of Technology to lead and shape the Sovereign Tech Agency’s technology and research strategy.

title: Endorsing a statement on European memory safety
content:
BSI and the Sovereign Tech Agency are endorsing "Improving Europe's cybersecurity posture through memory safety," which calls for more support for the large-scale adoption of memory-safe technology.

In an increasingly digital world, software bugs are no longer merely technical issues, they can be security challenges of strategic significance. Memory safety is a key security area, ensuring that software handles memory correctly and avoids errors like buffer overflows, which can create major security vulnerabilities.

title: Newsletter: Sovereign Tech Standards network kicks off, international collaboration on open digital infrastructure, hiring & more

Ten open source maintainers are part of the Sovereign Tech Standards network! By taking part in the development of open standards, they will help shape more secure and more interoperable technology. title: International policy network for open digital infrastructure kicks off
content:
Critical digital infrastructure spans the globe, and governing, funding and sustaining it requires international cooperation. That’s why the Sovereign Tech Agency proposed a new policy network to the Internet Governance Forum that's dedicated to this issue. It is now starting its work and you can join in.

Open digital infrastructure is foundational to modern society and the global economy: businesses, civil society, and the public sector increasingly rely on shared digital components, from core internet protocols and operating systems to software libraries or package repositories. Yet these basic technologies are often underfunded and under-resourced, and governance is fragmented across national jurisdictions and stakeholder communities. Open digital infrastructure transcends national borders, and sustaining it requires global cooperation across nearly every area of digital policy. The need for coordinated, multi-stakeholder approaches to address these challenges has never been more urgent.

title: Meet the First Sovereign Tech Standards Cohort
content:
Ten open source maintainers make up the first cohort of the Sovereign Tech Standards network. They are bringing hands-on expertise from critical open source infrastructure into standards development, helping shape better, more secure, and more interoperable technology.

Too often, open source maintainers aren't part of standards development, even though these standards directly shape the critical software components they build and maintain. But maintainers have something that's frequently missing from standards processes: direct open source implementation experience. They build, test, and operate software that has to conform to these specifications, giving them first-hand insight into real-world implementations. Standards developed without that perspective risk being less robust, less interoperable, and less reflective of how modern software actually works.
